narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 78% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influence. Placing in the bottom decile both times—compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students—strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. This low standing signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your LSAT score of 26, well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants, was the next most important factor and further increased the predicted risk of failure. In contrast, your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 worked mildly in your favor because it was only slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, giving a small push toward passing. However, this positive effect was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings and LSAT.

Your family income, full-time status, gender, and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Consider a post-baccalaureate program or additional coursework that demonstrates consistent high achievement before reapplying.
